title: U.S. Senators Reject Trump's War Powers Limit
text:
U.S. Senators Reject Trump’s War Powers Limit
U.S. Congressmen demanded a clear justification of the objectives of the operation against Iran and greater transparency. Photo: EFE.
March 4, 2026 Hour: 10:50 pm
The U.S. Senate failed to pass a resolution on war powers aimed at stemming President Donald Trump’s attacks on Iran.
The United States Senate on Wednesday, March 4, rejected a resolution aimed at limiting President Donald Trump’s military actions against Iran, amidst a rapidly escalating regional conflict that has already claimed hundreds of lives and prompted Tehran to launch a significant counteroffensive against Israel and U.S. strategic sites in West Asia.
RELATED: Iran Warns of Regional Repercussions From U.S.-Israeli War
The proposed resolution, which would have compelled the President to end any unauthorized military intervention within 30 days, except in direct defense of the United States, its territories, citizens, or armed forces, was defeated with 48 votes in favor and 52 against, highlighting a deep division within U.S. lawmakers regarding the extent of presidential authority in initiating and sustaining military engagements, particularly in the volatile Middle East.
The outcome grants the Trump administration continued broad discretion in its handling of the escalating tensions with Iran, a stance that has drawn sharp criticism from a segment of Congress.
Following the onset of what has been described as an U.S.-Israeli aggression, Democrat Party legislators vehemently criticized the Trump Administration, accusing it of circumventing constitutional requirements and significantly increasing the risks of a broader conflict escalation after recent attacks. These lawmakers demanded a clear justification for the objectives of the operation against Iran and greater transparency before both the Congress and the U.S. people.
Concerns intensified after a confidential briefing held on Tuesday with high-ranking officials, where Democratic senators alerted that the Republican President was not ruling out the deployment of ground troops to Iranian territory.
Regional Tensions Soar
The regional escalation commenced on February 28, when the United States and Israel executed coordinated attacks against Iran, less than 48 hours after the conclusion of the third round of indirect negotiations on the Iranian nuclear program in Geneva.
These bombings tragically resulted in the assassination of Iran’s Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, along with members of his family and several high-ranking civilian and military officials. This act marked a critical turning point, propelling the region into an unprecedented level of confrontation and significantly altering the geopolitical landscape.
In direct response to these attacks, Iran has intensified its retaliatory strikes against Israel and United States military bases located in Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, and Kuwait.
The Iranian Ministry of Health reported that the attacks carried out by the United States and Israel caused the deaths of nearly 930 people in Iran and left more than 6,180 injured. Conversely, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) informed that over 680 U.S. and Israeli personnel have either lost their lives or sustained injuries since the beginning of the Iranian counteroffensive, underscoring the severity and reciprocal nature of the current hostilities.
Adding another layer of complexity and potential global impact, Tehran also announced its full control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz, effectively banning transit through this crucial maritime route for global hydrocarbon trade. This bold action highlights Iran’s determination to respond forcefully to aggressions and demonstrates its capacity to significantly impact the global economy within a context of escalating conflict.
The U.S. Senate’s decision, therefore, comes amidst a backdrop of profound regional instability and growing international alarm.
Author: Laura V. Mor
Source: Agencies
